AbstractText.Label: CONTEXT
AbstractText.content: There has been a sustained debate in the medical literature over whether or not physicians should engage with patients' religious and spiritual concerns.

AbstractText.Label: OBJECTIVES
AbstractText.content: This study explores what physicians believe about the relative importance and appropriateness of engaging with patients' spiritual concerns and physicians' choices.

AbstractText.Label: METHODS
AbstractText.content: In 2010, a questionnaire was mailed to 2,016 U.S. physicians with survey items querying about the relative importance of addressing patients' spiritual concerns at the end of life and the appropriateness of interventions in addressing those concerns. The survey also contained an experimental vignette to assess physicians' willingness, if asked by patients, to participate in prayer.

AbstractText.Label: RESULTS
AbstractText.content: Adjusted response rate was 62% (1156/1878). The majority of physicians (65%) believe that it is essential to good practice for physicians to address patients' spiritual concerns at the end of life. Physicians who were more religious were more likely to believe that spiritual care is essential to good medical practice (Odds ratio [OR] 2.76, 95% Confidence Interval [CI] 1.12-6.81) and believe it is appropriate to always encourage patients to talk to a chaplain (OR: 5.71, 95% CI: 2.28-14.3). A majority of the physicians (55%) stated that, if asked, they would join the family and patient in prayer. Physicians' willingness to join ranged from 67% when there was concordance between the physician's and the patient's religious affiliation and 51% when there was discordance.

AbstractText.Label: CONCLUSION
AbstractText.content: The majority of U.S. physicians endorse a limited role in the provision of spiritual care, though opinions varied based on physicians' religious characteristics.
